Ahimelech
uh-HIM-eh-lek
proper noun (a priest of Nob)
Hebrew 'Achimelek, “brother of the king” or “my brother is king,” from 'ach (brother) and melek (king); the priest of Nob who aided the fleeing David.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ahimelech was the priest of Nob, son of Ahitub, who received the fleeing David and, not knowing the full breach between David and Saul, gave him the hallowed shewbread to eat and the sword of Goliath that was kept there. David came to him alone and hungry, and Ahimelech, though afraid, inquired of the LORD for him and supplied his need. But Doeg the Edomite, Saul's herdman, was present that day and reported the kindness to the king. Saul, in murderous rage, summoned Ahimelech and the priests of Nob and charged them with conspiracy; when his own guard would not lift a hand against the priests of the LORD, Doeg fell upon them and slew fourscore and five men that wore the linen ephod, and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword. Only Abiathar, Ahimelech's son, escaped to David. David confessed his own part: “I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house.” The dictionary marks Ahimelech as a witness to the cost of standing near the LORD's anointed in an evil day, and to the savagery of a king abandoned by the Spirit of God. His death fulfilled the long-pronounced judgment on the house of Eli, and his innocent blood cried against Saul and Doeg, whose end the LORD repaid.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The priest of Nob who gave the fleeing David the shewbread and Goliath's sword; for this kindness Saul, through Doeg the Edomite, massacred him and the priests of Nob, his son Abiathar alone escaping.

AHIMELECH, proper noun. [Hebrew, “brother of the king.”] The priest of Nob, son of Ahitub.

He received the fleeing David and gave him the hallowed shewbread (1 Samuel 21:6).

He also gave David the sword of Goliath, kept at Nob.

Doeg the Edomite reported it, and Saul ordered the priests slain (1 Samuel 22:18).

Only his son Abiathar escaped the massacre of Nob to flee to David.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Sa 21:1 — "Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee?"

1 Sa 21:6 — "So the priest gave him hallowed bread: for there was no bread there but the shewbread, that was taken from before the LORD, to put hot bread in the day when it was taken away."

1 Sa 22:18 — "And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod."

1 Sa 22:22 — "And David said unto Abiathar, I knew it that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to read the massacre of Nob as a tale of mere palace intrigue and miss the judgment of God and the cry of innocent blood.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness of innocent blood and the judgment of God. A secular reading takes the slaughter at Nob as palace politics—a paranoid king eliminating a perceived threat. Scripture frames it as something graver: the shedding of the blood of the priests of the LORD, a savagery the king's own soldiers would not commit, executed by a foreigner with no fear of God. The blood of Ahimelech and his house cried out, and the LORD did not leave it unavenged.

The account also displays the deepening ruin of a man abandoned by the Spirit of God. Saul, who once prophesied among the prophets, now murders the priests of God on a false charge of conspiracy. The dictionary marks the descent: rebellion unrepented hardens into cruelty, and the king who would not obey the voice of the LORD against Amalek now slays the LORD's own ministers. Ahimelech's death also fulfilled the ancient word against the house of Eli, that it should be cut off—a sober proof that the judgments of God, though they tarry, surely come.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew 'ach (brother) and melek (king), “brother of the king”; a priest of the line of Eli through Ahitub, serving at the sanctuary of Nob.

expand to see more

'Achimelek, Hebrew, “brother of the king” or “my brother is king.”

Son of Ahitub, of the priestly house of Eli.

Priest at Nob, “the city of the priests” (1 Samuel 22:19).

The shewbread (Hebrew lechem ha-panim, “bread of the presence”) he gave David.

Father of Abiathar, the sole survivor of the massacre of Nob.

Usage

"The pastor preached Ahimelech to show the cost of kindness to the LORD's anointed in an evil day."

"He marked the cry of innocent blood at Nob, which God repaid upon Saul and Doeg."

"She saw in the massacre the fulfilment of the long judgment pronounced on the house of Eli."
